identity.title: Test of skew (alternate cover test; vertical ocular misalignment)

technique.how: Patient fixates a target at about 1 m; alternately cover each eye every 1–2 s and watch the just-uncovered eye for a vertical re-fixation movement (one eye drifts up, the other down). Any vertical corrective movement = skew deviation; note head tilt and ocular counter-roll (ocular tilt reaction). Perform as the 'S' of HINTS in acute vestibular syndrome.
technique.prerequisites: Adequate vision and fixation in both eyes; continuous vertigo with nystagmus (acute vestibular syndrome) — HINTS is not validated for episodic or positional dizziness.
technique.contraindications: Uninterpretable with pre-existing strabismus, ocular motor palsy, internuclear ophthalmoplegia or an uncooperative patient.

interpretation.positive_finding: Vertical misalignment on alternate cover in AVS indicates a central (usually brainstem) lesion — LR+ about 6 — and overrides a 'peripheral-looking' abnormal head impulse test. A complete ocular tilt reaction was seen only with brainstem strokes.
interpretation.negative_finding: Absence of skew barely lowers stroke probability (LR− 0.78; sensitivity 25–27%) and misses most pure cerebellar infarcts. Rely on the full HINTS battery, not skew alone.
interpretation.pitfalls: Insensitive, especially for cerebellar (PICA) strokes; congenital or decompensated phorias, fourth-nerve palsy and old strabismus give false positives. Subtle skews need a trained examiner, and an untestable skew counts as a 'dangerous' HINTS result.
interpretation.changes_what: Skew present → treat as central AVS: stroke pathway, MRI-DWI, neurology; skew absent → no reassurance alone, complete HINTS (head impulse, nystagmus).

estimates.target_condition: Central lesion (69 ischemic strokes, 4 hemorrhages, 3 other) in acute vestibular syndrome — skew deviation present or untestable on prism cross-cover test
estimates.population: 101 consecutive high-risk AVS patients (≥1 stroke risk factor), 76 central / 25 peripheral, single academic stroke centre, examined generally <72 h from onset
estimates.reference_standard: MRI-DWI or CT for stroke; normal MRI plus clinical follow-up (most with caloric testing) for peripheral lesions
estimates.computed_from: Table 1 gives finding frequency 4% in 25 peripheral and 25% in 76 central patients and NLR 0.78 (0.67–0.91) as reported; specificity = 1 − 0.04 = 0.96; LR+ = 0.25/0.04 = 6.25 (computed from rounded percentages). Prevalence = 76/101 in a risk-enriched cohort.
estimates.location: Table 1 (PMC4593511 full text), columns PAVS n=25 / CAVS n=76 / NLR Central (95% CI)

estimates.target_condition: Structural brainstem involvement in acute vestibular syndrome — skew deviation evident at initial examination (subgroup; pure cerebellar lesions 4%)
estimates.population: Same cohort: 50 patients with brainstem involvement vs 25 with peripheral vestibulopathy (APV); 24 pure cerebellar lesions reported separately
estimates.reference_standard: MRI-DWI/CT lesion localization; clinical follow-up for peripheral lesions
estimates.computed_from: 15/50 brainstem cases with skew = 0.30; 1/25 APV with skew → specificity 0.96; LR+ = 0.30/0.04 = 7.5; LR− = 0.70/0.96 = 0.73.
estimates.quote: Skew was evident in 4% (n=1/25) with APV, 4% (n=1/24) with pure cerebellar lesions, and 30% (n=15/50) with demonstrated structural brainstem involvement
estimates.location: Results, paragraph on skew deviation (PMC4593511 full text)

estimates.target_condition: Central cause of acute vestibular syndrome — test of skew positive; pooled sensitivity only (specificity reported as 'high' but numeric value in supplementary Table 2, not accessible)
estimates.population: Systematic review of 10 study cohorts (n=800) of adults with AVS; results stratified by examiner type and stroke location
estimates.reference_standard: Neuroimaging (MRI-DWI) with clinical follow-up as used in primary studies
estimates.quote: considerably lower for the other tests including the test of skew (27.0% [16.1-37.9])
estimates.location: Results, 'Diagnostic accuracy of individual bedside tests' paragraph (PMC10524166 full text)

sources.citation: Kattah JC, Talkad AV, Wang DZ, Hsieh YH, Newman-Toker DE. HINTS to diagnose stroke in the acute vestibular syndrome: three-step bedside oculomotor examination more sensitive than early MRI diffusion-weighted imaging. Stroke 2009.

Tarnutzer AA, Gold D, Wang Z, Robinson KA, Kattah JC, Mantokoudis G et al. Impact of Clinician Training Background and Stroke Location on Bedside Diagnostic Test Accuracy in the Acute Vestibular Syndrome - A Meta-Analysis. Annals of neurology 2023.

Tarnutzer AA, Berkowitz AL, Robinson KA, Hsieh YH, Newman-Toker DE. Does my dizzy patient have a stroke? A systematic review of bedside diagnosis in acute vestibular syndrome. CMAJ : Canadian Medical Association journal = journal de l'Association medicale canadienne 2011. CMAJ 2011;183(9):E571-92; no OA body text and no abstract via PubMed fetch — cited for context only.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Not for episodic or positional dizziness without nystagmus, and never as a stand-alone rule-out.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Any HINTS 'dangerous' sign (normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, skew) → stroke work-up even when CT or early MRI is negative (MRI-DWI falsely negative in 12% <48 h, PMID 19762709, Abstract).
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Skew-specific reliability not reported. HINTS specificity was higher among subspecialists than non-subspecialists (97.6% vs 89.1%, p = 0.007) (PMID 37038843, Abstract).

extraction_notes: Anchors confirmed: Kattah 2009 (PMID 19762709; PMC4593511 OA text read, Table 1 row and Results paragraph quoted) and Tarnutzer 2011 CMAJ (PMID 21576300; PMC3114934 abstract-only deposit, PubMed fetch returned an empty abstract, so its pooled skew numbers could not be quoted and it carries no estimate). Added Tarnutzer 2023 Ann Neurol meta-analysis (PMID 37038843; PMC10524166 OA) — its Table 3 lists HINTS/HIT composites only; the skew-specific pooled sensitivity appears in Results text and pooled specificity is in supplementary Table 2 (not accessible), hence sensitivity-only third estimate. Estimate 1 uses the Table 1 row 'present or untestable' (3 untestable central patients counted as positive, per footnote §); estimate 2 uses skew 'evident' by lesion site from Results text. Specificity and LR+ are computed from rounded percentages (1/25 = 4%), so LR+ carries no CI. Kattah population was risk-enriched (75% central), so prevalence does not generalize to unselected ED dizziness. Composite HINTS accuracy (100% sens/96% spec single-study; pooled 95.3%/92.6%) deliberately not entered as a skew estimate (COMPOSITE rule).
